title: LLM.int8(): 8-bit Matrix Multiplication for Transformers at Scale
authors: Tim Dettmers, Mike Lewis, Younes Belkada, Luke Zettlemoyer

pages.title: Run 175B-parameter models in 8-bit with zero quality loss

blocks.html: Before LLM.int8(), running a 175B-parameter model required ~350GB of GPU memory in fp16 — spread across 8+ A100 80GB GPUs. Inference cost was prohibitive for almost everyone outside a few large labs.

Naive int8 quantization (uniformly map fp16 → int8) loses 15-30 points of perplexity at this scale and produces garbled outputs. The conventional wisdom by 2022 was that very large models simply couldn't be 8-bit quantized.

LLM.int8() identifies why naive quantization fails (a specific class of emergent outlier features) and proposes a mixed-precision matmul that handles outliers in fp16 and the rest in int8. Result: zero degradation in zero-shot performance for models up to 175B parameters, while halving memory.
Quantization compresses each weight (or activation) from 16-bit floating point to 8-bit integer:
You store the int8 tensor plus a scaling constant. Matmuls run in int8 (faster, half the memory, supported by NVIDIA Tensor Cores), then dequantize to fp16 for the next layer's normalization.

The problem: int8 only has 256 distinct levels. If your tensor has a few values with huge magnitude and most with tiny magnitude, the small values all quantize to the same bucket — information is destroyed.

The paper's key empirical finding: starting around the 6.7B parameter scale, Transformers develop a small number of emergent outlier features — hidden-state dimensions whose values are systematically much larger (sometimes 20× larger) than the rest.

items: They are sparse: ~0.1% of feature dimensions across the model.
They are systematic: the same dimensions consistently produce outliers across different inputs.
They are critical: zeroing them out (rather than quantizing) collapses model quality. So you can't just clip them.
They emerge abruptly with scale: small models don't have them; large models do.

blocks.html: Standard int8 quantization tries to fit both the outliers and the normal-range values into 256 levels using one scale factor. The outliers dominate the scale, the normal values get crushed, and quality collapses.

pages.title: Outliers in fp16, everything else in int8

blocks.html: LLM.int8()'s solution: split each matrix multiplication into two paths based on input features:

items: Identify the outlier columns of the input (a small constant fraction, typically 0.1%-1%).
Compute those columns' matmul in fp16 — accurate, but cheap because the slice is tiny.
Compute everything else in int8 with row-wise quantization for the weights and column-wise quantization for the activations (vector-wise rather than tensor-wise scaling preserves resolution).

blocks.html: This is implemented as a custom CUDA kernel. The fp16 path's overhead is small because outliers are sparse; the int8 path provides the memory and speed gains.

Measured on OPT models (125M to 175B) across a battery of zero-shot tasks (LAMBADA, PIQA, HellaSwag, WinoGrande). LLM.int8() matches fp16 quality at every scale tested. Naive int8 quantization degrades sharply above 6.7B.
Memory: ~50% reduction at inference. Speed: comparable to fp16 (int8 is faster per matmul but the mixed-precision path adds overhead). The win is memory and accessibility, not raw throughput.
Released as the bitsandbytes library — now standard in HuggingFace Transformers as load_in_8bit=True.

Before LLM.int8(), running 30B+ models locally required serious hardware. After, a single 24GB consumer GPU could load OPT-30B; two could load OPT-66B. This enabled the open-source LLM movement to actually run the big models the community was sharing.

Direct descendants: GPTQ (post-training 4-bit quantization), QLoRA (which builds on bitsandbytes' int4 for the frozen base during fine-tuning), AWQ, EXL2. The line from LLM.int8() through QLoRA is the technical foundation for the entire 2023-2024 era of open-source fine-tuning at home.
